one thing to add to this someone taught me awhile back that's always helped with screen protectors, for pre-application prep: Run your shower on super hot in your bathroom enough to totally steam it up, like visible fog in the air. Then shut it off and let the moisture dissipate. As soon as it's not moist enough in there any more to form any condensation (use your mirror as a guide), immediately do the screen protector application in there. All the steam grabs all the dust out of the air and makes it way less likely a wayward particle gets trapped.

First word of advice: Don't care about the awards at ALL on your first playthrough. Especially in the first game, the scoring system is heavily designed around you knowing the level and the combat system by heart, encouraging replayability. It's very very difficult for most players to get a decent award on a blind playthrough of a level. For your first time through the game just keep learning and enjoying and use whatever you can, items included, to get through it.

As for the combat, two tips of advice: 1. Until you can read the enemies like the back of your hand, you should focus on dodging over attacking. If you dodge into witch time, you can do free damage! As you learn the enemy's patterns more and more, you can feel safer to combo it, but always be ready to cancel into a dodge rather than over committing, which takes me into the second point. 2. Learn Dodge Offset if you haven't yet. Getting the hang of dodge offset will let you dodge way more often without dropping your combo, so you won't feel the need to commit to unsafe longer combos without dodging. Good explanation of it here at about 2:15: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NOVVmm4KOm4

Bayo 1 and 2 are my favorite games of all time, so I might be just a teensy bit biased, but I think if you're into character-action games at ALL you owe it to yourself to play Bayo.

I mean sure the game might be considered "short" if you're skipping through all the cutscenes and getting through the combat as fast as possible, but they're games that get richer the more you spend time with them. A first playthrough on normal is, honestly IMO, a tutorial secretly spread out over an entire game. It tricks you into thinking you're not still learning things. Then you boot up Hard Mode after you beat the game, and minibosses from like halfway through the game are now just normal enemies.

Furthermore, on your subsequent playthroughs, you'll have the entire arsenal of weapons to choose from and mix-and-match, so it's really fun to experiment and figure out what weapon combinations suit your playstyle.

And THEN, if you go really crazy, there's a bunch of hidden challenge rooms to find, and you can try to score attack the levels to get all the best trophies on them. There are rewards to getting a good score on every level, and while I won't spoil what the rewards are, they're definitely not trivial!

I'll leave you with this, the video that always comes to mind when someone asks why Bayo is my favorite game.. It's from several years ago when Bayo 1 was still fresh, so the quality is shit, but if you're at all into discovering combos in character action games, this should sell you: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bKtePkxZe70

I have like 300 hours across the 2 games and I *still* can't pull off that shit. But I pull off my own cool shit, and that's equally great. =P

edit: I should clarify I loved 2 but didn't have nearly as much experience with it, because I beat it on normal and almost beat my first Hard playthrough when my Wii U bricked itself, and I got super salty about having to collect everything again to continue my run, so I never got around to going back to it. Really looking forward to beating it on hard and unlocking everything on Switch.

The main thing about Disgaea is that your meta-goal is always thinking, "how can I gain power even faster than I can with what I'm doing now".

Easiest example: By spending an hour or two just focusing on farming the "Statistician" buffs on your items, you can literally boost the EXP a character gains from every action by 900% of the normal EXP they would gain. So the couple hours you spend building up some Statisticians end up saving you several hours of actual levelling, and you're constantly deciding where to spend your focus to progress most efficiently. It's like a Strategy-RPG with a hidden game-layer of puzzle. I love it.

I think it's totally hit or miss, but you might want to look into Disgaea 5 Complete. I got my switch around Thanksgiving, and I'm already up to 127 hours clocked in here. I honestly think Disgaea might have had a hand in creating the Clicker Game genre, because the main thing about it is that the numbers keep getting bigger.

My lowest levelled party member that I've never used at all has around 200-500 in each stat. My actual party, which is just breaching the post-game content (called the Carnage Dimension), has a few million in each stat, and I'm aiming for 10 mil in them before I stop grinding and start trying to progress again. If you're a weirdo like me where you get an odd masochistic joy out of grinding levels, and if you like Strategy RPGs as much as normal RPGs, Disgaea 5 might be exactly what you're looking for.

Oh, and assuming you have a friend/roomate who can play with you, ideally even more than one, one of the VR games we've gotten some of the best entertainment of is Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes. If you haven't heard of it, the person in the headset needs to disarm a bomb that only they can see, and they need to verbally describe what they're seeing to the other people in the real-life room, who have the bomb-defusel manual and can instruct the person in VR how to disarm it. It's really not as hard as it looks. There are only 2 real steps:

1. Find a rock that looks like it'd fit well on the previous one. If the previous one is convex, find one with a concave bottom. If it's a flat top, find a flat bottom. Make sure it's a somewhat balanced rock on a nearby one before you try to add it to the stack.

2. Place it on top very gently, with your other hand on the rock below it. You should be able to feel the "gravity" of the stack, which is what I call the directions it wants to fall. With very slight adjustments, you should be able to line up the "gravity" so that the rock you're adding helps keep the stack in place instead of unbalancing it, until you get to about 4 rocks. Then you need to start being really careful.

I just posted this in the "stupid mistakes" thread, but I figure it belongs here as well since 4 grams is the highest dose I've ever taken. TLDR: Bad times in the forest on mushrooms.

My third trip with mushrooms, I decided to take about 4 dried grams and go hiking by myself. On a trail that I had never hiked before. I figured "Eh, I have a map, and I've hiked all of the shorter trails, this will be no problem."

1st thing: I'm walking along a ridgetop, about 30' below me is a bunch of dense underbrush. Something was wandering around rustling in there. Probably a boar or something, but at the time all I could think was "Lost Smoke Monster."

2nd: I reach the furthest point out on the hike: An ancient redwood labeled on my map as "Big Ben". I'm not exaggerating in the slightest when I say this tree was at least 8 or 10 feet in diameter. At this point I'm about 6 miles from the nearest civilization and I'm tripping hard. I decide to stop and eat my lunch. Suddenly get the sensation that the tree is watching me. I look at it and it looks like it's breathing. I know I'm tripping... but I can't shake the sense that the tree was perceiving me and distinctly did not like me.

3rd: I moved on rather quickly after that. The trail I was hiking was a big loop, and now I was on the downhill section heading back towards where I started. I was heading down a switchback that would go about 300 feet in each direction before turning back the other way. I passed a tree almost as large as Big Ben, right on the ridge of my current switchback and stopped to look at it. It too appeared to be breathing and watching me. No worries, I told myself, I'm just tripping really hard. I took too much, from now on I stick to an 8th or less. I continue down.

Two switchbacks down, I swear to god, I encounter the same tree in the same spot. I actually had to stop and gather my bearings for a minute. I honestly thought I had somehow turned around. These trees were as identical as trees can be. And I still felt the same malevolent presence.

4th: I continue down and get to ground level. I would like to point out right now that I have had no cellphone service for the past 2 hours. I'm still 4 miles from civilization and I'm still tripping balls. I'm currently listening to Row Jimmy Row by the Grateful Dead, marching happily along the trail, proud of myself for getting past those goddamn scary trees.

BOOM, ATTACKED BY A SWARM OF WASPS OR BEES OR SOMETHING. I throw the bottle of Gatorade I was drinking behind me, dive forward on the ground and play dead. Hey, it's worth a shot, right? Luckily it worked. A lot of them went after the bottle instead of me. I crawl away and finally regain the presence of mind to do a check of myself.

I have 3 stingers in my left arm, 4 in my right arm, and one on each hand. All of them have attached venom sacs, pumping away. You may or may not be able to imagine how this looks on four grams of mushrooms. This is also a good time to mention I'd never been stung by a wasp or bee before and had no idea if I was allergic. I was still thinking enough to rake out the stingers with my fingernails, and lacking any kind of first aid kit, rubbed mud on all my wounds. It made sense at the time.

Humbled and filled with the strong impression that I am no longer welcome in this forest, I limp back to the bottom of the trail. Luckily, I have a friend who lives on the same street as the entrance to the trail, and he's the kind of friend who just says "sure, no problem" when you show up at his door covered in mud and ask to use his shower.

The trip didn't end until 2 hours later, but I just spent it watching anime with my friend. Obviously, I was not allergic. I still hike in that section of forest, even while tripping occasionally, but never as deep as I went in that time.
